\section[el alumno]{el alumno — the pupil, the student}

\label{lesson:ES-C476-alumno}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the material, then the Spanish for the gardener.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el alumno}
\textbf{el alumno} — \textquotedblleft{}the pupil, the student\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Cada alumno tiene un libro.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Each pupil has a book.}
\end{quote}

A girl or woman is \emph{la alumna}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el alumno}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el alumno}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el alumno}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the material, then the Spanish for the gardener, then say \emph{el alumno} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el alumno mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The pupil, the student\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[comprender]{comprender — to understand}

\label{lesson:ES-C476-comprender}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the pupil, then the Spanish for to practise.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: comprender}
\textbf{comprender} — \textquotedblleft{}to understand\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}

\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I do not understand the question.}
\end{quote}

A close twin of \emph{entender}, slightly more formal.

\section[aburrido]{aburrido — bored; boring}

\label{lesson:ES-C476-aburrido}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to understand, then the Spanish for the mistake.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aburrido}
\textbf{aburrido} — \textquotedblleft{}bored; boring\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La película es aburrida.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The film is boring.}
\end{quote}

With \emph{estar} it means bored (\emph{estoy aburrido}); with \emph{ser} it means boring (\emph{es aburrido}).

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{aburrido}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to understand, then the Spanish for the mistake, then say \emph{aburrido} again
\end{itemize}
